summary:
Kars province stands under the national framework of Turkey, and the sources underlying this record carry no statute, incident, court decision or enforcement record specific to Kars. The assessment for a trans visitor to Kars is therefore governed by the country-wide pattern documented below, with no evidence that provincial practice diverges from it in either direction.

Turkey's legal trajectory points toward further criminalisation. An October 2025 Human Rights Watch release reports a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals carrying out such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

The draft had not been enacted when reported, but its pending status has not stopped authorities from acting against the prohibitions it contains. Rights groups describe enforcement applied ahead of legislation in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring review finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people in Turkey became explicit state policy. "Year of the Family" instructions were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association was closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against eleven of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned. The report documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected group, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the previous year, and 299 detention decisions, alongside an overall total of roughly 313 violations, about 2.5 times the previous year's figure. Freedom-of-expression violations rose from 216 to 540.

Street-level enforcement illustrates how that policy operates on people who present outside expected norms. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés and held them at a police station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police imposed no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at checkpoints of this kind are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk whenever presentation does not match the gender marker on a passport.

The passport-carrying requirement compounds that exposure. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. In Kars, a province with heavy transit and border-adjacent movement, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners in Turkey are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated through Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, rights groups demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
tangentialFactors:
The sources are concentrated on Istanbul, Ankara and other major urban centres. Kars, in the north-east of the country, has no documented case of its own in this record, so the enforcement picture for a visitor there rests on national rules and national statistics rather than on observed local practice.

Turkey's administrative and health systems are centrally directed, which is why Health Ministry regulations and "Year of the Family" directives to public institutions are treated here as binding across provinces rather than as optional guidance. A circular issued by a provincial health directorate elsewhere in the country shows that provincial bodies implement national care policy, and there is no reason in the sources to assume Kars health authorities operate outside that chain.

Checkpoint and passport rules are national and apply to transit routes as well as urban centres, so the document-carrying obligation that creates outing risk in holiday destinations applies with equal force on routes through Kars.

The Sincan prison case is a national detention-condition matter rather than a local one; Turkey's practice of placing trans prisoners by registered sex operates through the national prison administration and is not confined to any single facility.

The leaked draft package had not been enacted at the time of reporting, and its final form and passage date are unresolved in the sources. Assessments that treat its contents as settled law would overstate the record; equally, monitoring evidence shows enforcement in the same direction while the draft remains pending.
